column2: A few spellings have been brought forward — publick to public, compleat to complete, shew to show, Chap. written out as Chapter, and the printer’s V for U in Vnbelief.
column3:
The spelling has been brought up to date, so that the book reads easily and sounds rightly when read aloud: publick is public, compleat is complete, untill is until, and the printer’s V for U in Vnbelief is set right. The keyed text of 1691 carried many slips of the hand, and these are mended; where a word or a few words had been lost, they are restored from William H. Goold’s printing of 1850 (The Works of John Owen, vol. I).

\n

This edition is lightly modernised, for clear reading and listening, not for interpretation. The old forms are given as we say them now (thou is you, hath is has), references and abbreviations are written out, and some long sentences are divided by punctuation. A few words whose meaning has changed since 1691 are given in the word we use now, with a lettered note showing the word he wrote; they are listed at the back under Words Brought Forward. The British spellings stand.

column2: Nothing is marked in the text itself — a reader should meet Owen, not our footnotes.
column3: Nothing else is marked in the text itself, so that a reader meets Owen and not our footnotes.

column2: • Scripture is left exactly as it was printed, capitals, spelling and all. Those words are not ours to modernise.
column3: • Scripture is quoted as the author quoted it. In a lightly modernised edition its old forms are brought forward with his (thou is you), and nothing else in it is changed.

column2: • The author’s own English is left alone. We may correct his spelling; we do not rewrite him. Thou, hath and doth stand.
column3: • The author’s own English is left alone. We may correct his spelling; we do not rewrite him. A lightly modernised edition brings his old forms forward as well (hath is has), and its About This Edition says exactly what was changed.
